#1
L: Upward-rooted, downward-branched, the aśvattha they call imperishable; whose leaves [are] the sacred hymns — who knows it, he [is] a knower of the Veda.
I: They speak of an imperishable aśvattha tree with its root above and its branches below, the hymns of the Veda its leaves; whoever knows this tree is one who truly knows the Veda.
N: Chapter 15 opens with no question from Arjuna; Kṛṣṇa continues speaking directly from chapter 14's close, at once introducing the celebrated image that runs through verses 1-4: the cosmic aśvattha (the sacred fig, Ficus religiosa) turned upside down, its root growing ūrdhvam, 'upward', and its branches adhaḥ, 'downward' — a figure the tradition (Śaṅkara) reads as saṃsāra, the tree of transmigratory existence rooted in the unmanifest above and branching down into the visible world, and already found at Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.1's ūrdhva-mūlo 'vāk-śākha eṣo 'śvatthaḥ sanātanaḥ. Chandāṃsi, 'the Vedic hymns', are its parṇāni, 'leaves' — an ornament and a protection, as leaves are to a tree, rather than the tree's essence, so that knowing the tree itself, not only its leaves, is what makes one a veda-vit, 'a knower of the Veda' in the fullest sense. Sandhi: ūrdhvamūlam adhaḥśākham aśvattham are three appositive words simply written joined, each final -m unaffected before what follows; prāhur avyayam is prāhuḥ+avyayam (-uḥ+a-→-ur a-); yas taṃ is yaḥ+tam (-aḥ+t-→-as t-).
#2
L: Below and above spread its branches, nourished-by-the-guṇas, having-sense-objects-as-sprouts; and below, roots stretched-out continuously, bound-to-action, in-the-world-of-men.
I: Its branches spread both downward and upward, nourished by the guṇas, putting out the sense objects as their tender shoots; and below, its roots stretch on without a break, binding one to action in the human world.
N: The tree-image continues (through verse 4): its śākhāḥ, 'branches', spread both adhaḥ and ūrdhvam, 'below and above', through every level of existence, guṇa-pravṛddhāḥ, 'nourished by the guṇas' (sattva, rajas and tamas of chapter 14, kept untranslated per convention), and putting forth viṣaya-pravālāḥ, 'sense-objects as their sprouts' — the branches' new growth is exactly what tempts and traps the senses. Secondary mūlāni, 'roots', spread continuously downward too, anubandhīni, 'entailing, binding one to', karman, 'action', in manuṣya-loke, 'the human world' — the ordinary world of ritual and worldly action, as against the tree's unseen root above. Sandhi: adhaścordhvaṃ packs adhaḥ+ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-) and ca+ūrdhvam (a+ū→o); prasṛtāstasya is prasṛtāḥ+tasya (-āḥ+t-→-ās t-); śākhā (visarga-less at the pāda's end) and guṇapravṛddhā (likewise) both show the visarga of an -āḥ ending silently dropping before a following voiced consonant (g-, v- respectively) — a pattern distinct from the more familiar -aḥ→-o of a short-a ending, and one that recurs through this chapter wherever a fem./masc. plural in -āḥ meets a voiced sound; adhaśca is adhaḥ+ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-); mūlānyanusaṃtatāni is mūlāni+anusaṃtatāni (-i+a-→-y a-); karmānubandhīni is karma+anubandhīni (a+a→ā).
#3
L: Its form is not perceived here in that way; nor an end, nor also a beginning, nor a foundation; this aśvattha, with-well-grown-roots, having cut with the firm weapon of non-attachment —
I: Its true form cannot be perceived here as it is; it has no end, no beginning, and no stable ground. Having cut down this aśvattha with its deep-grown roots, with the firm weapon of non-attachment —
N: This denies that the cosmic tree's rūpam, 'form' (its ultimate shape, as against its familiar appearance), can be grasped as it really is, and further denies it has anta, ādi, or saṃpratiṣṭhā — 'end', 'beginning', or 'foundation' — a set of negations recalling how the self/brahman is elsewhere described as beginningless and endless (e.g. 2.20's ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yam purāṇo); saṃsāra, pictured as this tree, has no discoverable starting point or bottom from within it. The sentence begun here runs on into verse 4: aśvattham enaṃ suvirūḍha-mūlam, 'this aśvattha with its roots grown deep and strong', must be cut down asaṅga-śastreṇa dṛḍhena, 'with the firm weapon of non-attachment' (asaṅga, echoing chapters 2-3's teaching that attachment, saṅga, is what binds action). Uniquely in this chapter (indeed in the whole poem), the compound suvirūḍha-mūlam is split by the pāda break itself: the source text (reproduced exactly here) ends this line with सुविरूढमूल- and begins the next with मसङ्गशस्त्रेण, so that the word's final -m, fused by ordinary sandhi with the following asaṅga-, falls on the far side of the line/word-token boundary — an authentic feature of the transmitted text, not a misprint, and so left untouched. Sandhi: rūpamasyeha packs rūpam+asya (simply joined, -m unaffected before the vowel) and asya+iha (a+i→e); tathopalabhyate is tathā+upalabhyate (ā+u→o); nānto is na+antaḥ (a+a→ā), whose own -aḥ before n-→-o; cādirna packs ca+ādiḥ (a+ā→ā) and ādiḥ+na (-iḥ+n-→-ir n-).
#4
L: Thence, that state must be sought, into which, having gone, they do not return again; that very primal Person I take refuge in, from whom the ancient activity has issued forth.
I: Then that state must be sought out, from which those who reach it never return; I take refuge in that same primal Person, from whom this age-old outgoing activity first issued.
N: This completes the sentence begun in verses 3-4 (chittvā, 'having cut', governs what follows): once the tree of saṃsāra is felled with non-attachment, tataḥ, 'thence', one must seek out padam, 'that state', from which yasmin gatāḥ na nivartanti bhūyaḥ, 'having gone into which they do not return again' — the same promise made of liberation at 8.21's yaṃ prāpya na nivartante. That state is identified with tam eva ca ādyam puruṣam, 'that very primal Person' (puruṣa, translated throughout this pipeline as 'the Person', following the convention set at chapters 8, 10-11 and 13, rather than left untranslated), in whom Kṛṣṇa says he takes refuge (prapadye) — speaking, in effect, of himself in the third person as yataḥ, 'the one from whom', purāṇī pravṛttiḥ, 'the ancient/primeval activity', has issued forth, recalling the cosmogony of 14.3-4's seed placed in the great brahman. Sandhi: yasmingatā is yasmin+gatāḥ, simply written joined (the nasal unaffected before the consonant g-); cādyaṃ is ca+ādyam (a+ā→ā).
#5
L: Free-from-pride-and-delusion, having-conquered-the-fault-of-attachment, ever-intent-on-the-inner-self, their-desires-withdrawn, freed from the dualities called pleasure-and-pain, the-undeluded go to that imperishable state.
I: Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the taint of attachment, ever fixed on the inner self, their desires stilled, freed from the dualities known as pleasure and pain — the undeluded reach that imperishable state.
N: This continues the sentence begun in verses 3-4, now describing, in a long run of compounds, those who actually reach the imperishable padam named at the end of verse 4: they are nirmāna-mohāḥ, 'free of pride and delusion'; jita-saṅga-doṣāḥ, 'having conquered the fault of attachment' (recalling the saṅga just cut away by the asaṅga-śastra of verse 3); adhyātma-nityāḥ, 'ever intent on the inner self' (adhyātma named already at 8.3); vinivṛtta-kāmāḥ, 'their desires withdrawn'; and dvandvaiḥ vimuktāḥ sukha-duḥkha-saṃjñaiḥ, 'freed from the dualities called pleasure and pain' (the same confusion of opposites named at 7.27-28). As at verse 3, the source splits a compound across the pāda break: sukha-duḥkha-saṃjñaiḥ, at the line's end, is completed by the -r- that begins the next line (from -aiḥ+g-→-air g-, before gacchanti), again an authentic feature of the transmitted text reproduced here as given. Amūḍhāḥ, 'the undeluded', is the subject of gacchanti, 'go' (understood also with all the preceding predicate adjectives), reaching padam avyayam tat, 'that imperishable state' first named in verse 4. Sandhi: gacchantyamūḍhāḥ is gacchanti+amūḍhāḥ (-i+a-→-y a-).
#6
L: That, the sun illumines not, nor the moon, nor fire; having gone to which they do not return — that [is] my supreme abode.
I: Neither the sun nor the moon nor fire illumines that place; having reached it, none return — that is my supreme abode.
N: This describes the imperishable padam of verses 4-5 further: it is beyond illumination by any of the great luminaries — sūrya, 'the sun', śaśāṅka, 'the moon' (literally 'hare-marked', from the mark seen on its face), and pāvaka, 'fire' — because it is itself self-luminous, closely echoing Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15 and Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14's na tatra sūryo bhāti na candra-tārakam. Kṛṣṇa now names it directly as tat dhāma paramam mama, 'that, my supreme abode', identifying the destination of verses 4-5 as his own. Sandhi: sūryo na is sūryaḥ+na (-aḥ before n-→-o); śaśāṅko na is śaśāṅkaḥ+na (-aḥ before n-→-o); yad gatvā is yat+gatvā (-t+g-→-d g-); tad dhāma is tat+dhāma (-t+dh-→-d dh-).
#7
L: An eternal fragment of me alone, in the world of living beings, becomes a living soul; it draws to itself the senses, with mind as sixth, abiding in nature.
I: An eternal fragment of myself alone becomes, in the world of living beings, an individual soul, and draws to itself the senses — with the mind as the sixth — that are seated in nature.
N: This opens a new section (through verse 11) that turns from the impersonal tree-image to the individual jīva, 'living soul': it is Kṛṣṇa's own aṃśaḥ, 'a part, a fragment', sanātanaḥ, 'eternal', though appearing as jīva-bhūtaḥ, 'become a living being' — the claim, taken up by later tradition as the doctrine of the jīva as an aṃśa of Īśvara, that the individual self differs from the Supreme not in kind but only as a portion embodied. Such a soul karṣati, 'draws' (or 'drags along'), the indriyāṇi, 'senses' — manaḥ-ṣaṣṭhāni, 'with mind as the sixth' (the five sense-organs plus manas, counted as a sixth, exactly as at 13.5's ekādaśa-indriyāṇi and 2.67's account of the senses dragging the mind) — which are themselves prakṛti-sthāni, 'seated in nature', not in the soul itself. Sandhi: mamaivāṃśo packs mama+eva (a+e→ai) and aṃśaḥ+jīvaloke (-aḥ before j-→-o); manaḥṣaṣṭhānīndriyāṇi packs manaḥ+ṣaṣṭhāni (visarga retained before ṣ-, as already at verse 1's adhaḥśākham) and ṣaṣṭhāni+indriyāṇi (-i+i-→-ī-, vowel lengthening of like vowels).
#8
L: The body which he obtains, and which the lord departs from, having seized these [senses], he goes along [with them] — as the wind [carries] scents from their resting-place.
I: As the lord — the embodied soul — takes up a body, and as it departs from one, it takes these senses along and goes on its way, just as the wind carries scents away from their resting place, a flower.
N: This describes how the jīva of verse 7 passes from body to body: īśvaraḥ (here 'the lord, the ruling one' — the individual soul as controller of its own body and senses, not the Supreme Lord) yat śarīram avāpnoti, 'the body it acquires', and yat [śarīrāt] ca api utkrāmati, 'and [the body] it also departs from', in both cases takes gṛhītvā, 'having seized', etāni, 'these' [the senses named in verse 7] along with it, saṃyāti, 'proceeding on', vāyuḥ gandhān iva āśayāt, 'like the wind carrying scents away from their resting place' — a well-known simile, already glossed this way by Śaṅkara, of the subtle senses borne along by the departing soul as a breeze carries a flower's fragrance from the flower itself. Sandhi: yadavāpnoti is yat+avāpnoti (-t+a-→-d a-, a stop voiced before a vowel); yaccāpyutkrāmatīśvaraḥ packs yat+ca (-t+c-→-c c-, assimilation), ca+api (a+a→ā), api+utkrāmati (-i+u-→-y u-), and utkrāmati+īśvaraḥ (-i+ī-→-ī-, vowel lengthening); gṛhītvaitāni is gṛhītvā+etāni (ā+e→ai); vāyurgandhāniva is vāyuḥ+gandhān (-uḥ+g-→-ur g-), gandhān+iva simply joined; ivāśayāt is iva+āśayāt (a+ā→ā).
#9
L: The ear, the eye, touch, and taste, and smell too, and, governing the mind, this [soul] partakes of the sense-objects.
I: Taking control of the ear, the eye, touch, taste, and smell, and the mind as well, this soul enjoys the objects of the senses.
N: This continues verse 8's description of the embodying soul, naming the six faculties it governs (adhiṣṭhāya, 'having taken control of, presiding over'): the five senses — śrotra (hearing), cakṣus (sight), sparśana (touch), rasana (taste), ghrāṇa (smell) — plus manas, 'the mind', the sixth already named at verse 7's manaḥ-ṣaṣṭhāni; through them ayam, 'this [soul]', upasevate, 'partakes of, resorts to', viṣayān, 'the sense-objects'. Sandhi: ghrāṇameva is ghrāṇam+eva, simply joined, -m unaffected before the vowel; manaścāyam packs manaḥ+ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-) and ca+ayam (a+a→ā).
#10
L: [Whether] departing, or remaining, or enjoying [the senses], united-with-the-guṇas — the deluded do not perceive [it]; those-with-the-eye-of-knowledge perceive [it].
I: The deluded do not perceive the soul as it departs, or stays, or enjoys the senses, united with the guṇas; but those who have the eye of knowledge do perceive it.
N: This closes the section on the embodied soul (verses 7-10) by contrasting two kinds of perceiver: the vimūḍhāḥ, 'the deluded', na anupaśyanti, 'do not perceive', the soul in any of its states — utkrāmantam, 'departing' (as at verse 8), sthitam, 'remaining [in the body]', or bhuñjānam, 'enjoying [the sense-objects]' (as at verse 9), guṇa-anvitam, 'joined with the guṇas' (the very guṇas whose interplay chapter 14 described) — while jñāna-cakṣuṣaḥ, 'those who have the eye of knowledge' (a recurring Gītā image, cf. 13.34's jñāna-cakṣuṣā), paśyanti, 'do perceive' it, echoing 13.34's teaching that only knowledge, not the physical eye, discerns the field from its knower. Sandhi: vāpi is vā+api (ā+a→ā); guṇānvitam is guṇa+anvitam (a+a→ā); nānupaśyanti is na+anupaśyanti (a+a→ā); vimūḍhā, at the pāda's end, shows the same -āḥ elision before a following vowel (a- of anupaśyanti, across the pāda break) already noted at verse 2.
#11
L: Striving yogins perceive it, abiding within the self; but, even striving, the-unaccomplished, thoughtless [seekers] do not perceive it.
I: Yogins who strive perceive it dwelling within the self; but the unaccomplished, lacking discernment, do not perceive it, even though they strive.
N: This contrasts two kinds of strivers, sharpening verse 10's contrast of the deluded and the discerning: yatantaḥ yoginaḥ, 'yogins who strive', do paśyanti, 'perceive', enam [the soul] ātmani avasthitam, 'abiding within the self'; but even yatantaḥ api, 'even those who strive', if they are akṛta-ātmānaḥ, 'whose selves are unaccomplished, unperfected' (whose discipline has not yet borne fruit) and acetasaḥ, 'lacking discernment', na paśyanti, 'do not perceive' it — effort alone, without the ripening of insight, does not suffice, a qualification already implied at 6.44-45's account of the yogin still in training. Sandhi: yatanto is yatantaḥ, -aḥ before y-→-o; yoginaścainaṃ packs yoginaḥ+ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-) and ca+enam (a+e→ai); paśyantyātmanyavasthitam packs paśyanti+ātmani (-i+ā-→-y ā-) and ātmani+avasthitam (-i+a-→-y a-); yatanto'pyakṛtātmāno packs yatantaḥ+api (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha), api+akṛtātmānaḥ (-i+a-→-y a-), and akṛtātmānaḥ+na (-aḥ before n-→-o); nainaṃ is na+enam (a+e→ai); paśyantyacetasaḥ is paśyanti+acetasaḥ (-i+a-→-y a-).
#12
L: The radiance, residing-in-the-sun, that illumines the whole world, and that which [is] in the moon, and that which [is] in fire — know that radiance [to be] mine.
I: Know that the radiance residing in the sun, which lights up the whole world, and the radiance in the moon and in fire, is mine.
N: This opens a new section (through verse 15) in which Kṛṣṇa identifies himself with the powers pervading the natural world, beginning with tejaḥ, 'radiance, light': āditya-gatam, 'residing in the sun', it illumines jagat akhilam, 'the whole world', and the same tejaḥ is found candramasi, 'in the moon', and agnau, 'in fire' — recalling 10.21's ādityānām ahaṃ viṣṇuḥ and closely echoing Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15's na tatra sūryo bhāti, na candra-tārakaṃ nemā vidyuto bhānti kuto'yam agniḥ | tam eva bhāntam anubhāti sarvaṃ tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṃ vibhāti — the light of these bodies being itself derivative of the one true light. Sandhi: yadādityagataṃ is yat+āditya-gatam (-t+ā-→-d ā-); tejo is tejaḥ, -aḥ before j-→-o; jagadbhāsayate'khilam packs jagat+bhāsayate (-t+bh-→-d bh-) and bhāsayate+akhilam (-e+a-→-e' with avagraha); yaccandramasi and yaccāgnau both begin yat+ca (-t+c-→-c c-), the second further compounding ca+agnau (a+a→ā); tattejo packs tat+tejaḥ (-t+t-→-t t-, identical stops simply written together) and tejaḥ's own -aḥ before v-→-o.
#13
L: Having entered the earth, I sustain the creatures by [my] vigor; and I nourish all the plants, having become Soma, consisting of sap.
I: Having entered the earth, I sustain all creatures by my vigor; and, becoming the sap-giving Soma, I nourish all the plants.
N: This continues Kṛṣṇa's self-identification with the powers of nature: gām āviśya, 'having entered the earth' (gām here in the older sense 'the earth', not 'a cow'), he dhārayāmi bhūtāni ojasā, 'sustains all beings by [his] vigor' — the same idea of Kṛṣṇa as the hidden support of the physical world as verse 12's tejaḥ in sun, moon and fire; and, becoming somaḥ, 'Soma' (both the moon and the soma-plant/juice central to Vedic sacrifice, its two senses deliberately overlapping here), rasa-ātmakaḥ, 'consisting of sap, essence' (the vital sap that gives plants their nourishing power), he puṣṇāmi oṣadhīḥ sarvāḥ, 'nourishes all the plants' — traditionally read, with Śaṅkara, as an allusion to the moon's influence on plant growth. Sandhi: gāmāviśya is gām+āviśya, simply joined (-m before the vowel unaffected); dhārayāmyaham is dhārayāmi+aham (-i+a-→-y a-); ahamojasā is aham+ojasā, simply joined; cauṣadhīḥ is ca+oṣadhīḥ (a+o→au); somo is somaḥ, -aḥ before bh-→-o; rasātmakaḥ is rasa+ātmaka (a+ā→ā).
#14
L: I, having become Vaiśvānara, dwelling in the body of living beings, united-with-the-prāṇa-and-apāna-[breaths], digest the fourfold food.
I: I, becoming Vaiśvānara, the fire of digestion, dwelling in the bodies of living beings and joined with the breaths prāṇa and apāna, digest the four kinds of food.
N: This continues Kṛṣṇa's identification with nature's powers by turning to digestion: as vaiśvānaraḥ, 'Vaiśvānara' (literally 'belonging to all men', the fire common to every living body, here specifically the digestive fire), he dwells (āśritaḥ) in the deham, 'body', of prāṇinām, 'living beings', and, samāyuktaḥ, 'joined with', the prāṇa and apāna breaths (the upward and downward vital airs of yogic physiology, already invoked at 4.29-30 and 5.27), pacāmi annam catur-vidham, 'digests the fourfold food' — traditionally glossed by Śaṅkara as food that is chewed, sucked, licked and swallowed. Sandhi: vaiśvānaro is vaiśvānaraḥ, -aḥ before bh-→-o; dehamāśritaḥ is deham+āśritaḥ, simply joined; prāṇāpāna- is prāṇa+apāna (a+a→ā); pacāmyannaṃ is pacāmi+annam (-i+a-→-y a-).
#15
L: And I am seated in the heart of all [beings]; from me [come] memory, knowledge, and its loss; and by all the Vedas, I alone am to be known; and I alone [am] the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Veda.
I: I am seated in the hearts of all beings; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss; and I alone am what is to be known through all the Vedas — I am indeed the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Veda.
N: This closes the chapter's central self-revelatory section (verses 12-15) by moving from Kṛṣṇa's presence in nature to his presence within the knowing subject itself: sarvasya hṛdi saṃniviṣṭaḥ, 'seated in the heart of all beings' (echoing 13.17's sarvasya ca hṛdi sthitam), he is the source of both smṛtiḥ, 'memory', jñānam, 'knowledge', and apohanam, its own 'removal, forgetting' — claiming responsibility for the whole range of cognitive experience, favorable and unfavorable alike, as already at 10.10-11. He then declares himself vedyaḥ, 'the one to be known', through the Vedas collectively, and, in a striking pair of titles, both vedānta-kṛt, 'the author of the Vedānta' (the Upaniṣads, the concluding portion of Vedic revelation), and veda-vid, 'the knower of the Veda' — at once the source, the object, and the knower of all sacred learning. Sandhi: cāhaṃ is ca+aham (a+a→ā); saṃniviṣṭo is saṃniviṣṭaḥ, -aḥ before m-→-o; smṛtirjñānamapohanaṃ packs smṛtiḥ+jñānam (-iḥ+j-→-ir j-) and jñānam+apohanam, simply joined; vedaiśca is vedaiḥ+ca (-aiḥ+c-→-aiś c-); sarvairahameva packs sarvaiḥ+aham (-aiḥ+a-→-air a-) and aham+eva, simply joined; vedyo is vedyaḥ, -aḥ before v-→-o; vedāntakṛdvedavideva packs veda+anta (a+a→ā) and vedānta-kṛt+vedavid (-t+v-→-d v-); cāham is ca+aham (a+a→ā).
#16
L: These two Persons [are] in the world: the Perishable, and the Imperishable too. The Perishable [is] all beings; the unchanging [one] is called the Imperishable.
I: There are two Persons in this world, the Perishable and the Imperishable. The Perishable consists of all beings; the Imperishable is called the unchanging one.
N: This opens the chapter's climactic teaching (through verse 19), the doctrine that gives the chapter its name, Puruṣottama-yoga: two puruṣau, 'Persons' (puruṣa, translated 'the Person' throughout this pipeline, as at chapters 8, 10-11 and 13, rather than left untranslated), exist in the world — kṣaraḥ, 'the Perishable' (from kṣar, 'to flow, decay, perish'), identified with sarvāṇi bhūtāni, 'all [finite, changing] beings', and akṣaraḥ, 'the Imperishable' (the plain negation of kṣara; the same word elsewhere, unrelatedly, means 'a syllable', but not here), described as kūṭa-sthaḥ, 'standing on a summit, unmoving, unchanging' — the individual self in its unchanging aspect, as distinct from its ever-changing embodiments. Verses 17-18 go on to name a third, still higher reality beyond both. Sandhi: dvāvimau is dvau+imau (-au+i-→-āv i-); kṣaraścākṣara packs kṣaraḥ+ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-) and ca+akṣaraḥ (a+a→ā); akṣara eva shows the visarga of akṣaraḥ dropped before the vowel with the hiatus retained rather than coalescing to ai — an accepted option in epic verse, recurring at verse 18's akṣarād api; kūṭastho'kṣara packs kūṭasthaḥ+akṣaraḥ (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha).
#17
L: But the highest Person [is] another, declared [to be] the supreme self — who, having entered the three worlds, sustains [them], the imperishable Lord.
I: But there is another, the highest Person, called the Supreme Self — the imperishable Lord who, pervading the three worlds, sustains them.
N: This introduces the third and highest reality, beyond the kṣara-akṣara pair of verse 16: uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ, 'the highest Person', described as parama-ātmā, 'the Supreme Self' (a title used elsewhere of the innermost reality present in every being, e.g. 6.7, 13.22), and as avyayaḥ īśvaraḥ, 'the imperishable Lord' who, loka-trayam āviśya, 'having pervaded the three worlds' (earth, atmosphere and heaven), bibharti, 'sustains, upholds' them — anticipating the direct self-identification with this uttama-puruṣa that Kṛṣṇa makes in verses 18-19. Sandhi: puruṣastvanyaḥ packs puruṣaḥ+tu (-aḥ+t-→-as t-) and tu+anyaḥ (-u+a-→-v a-, yaṇ); paramātmetyudāhṛtaḥ packs parama+ātmā (a+ā→ā), ātmā+iti (ā+i→e), and iti+udāhṛtaḥ (-i+u-→-y u-); lokatrayamāviśya is loka-trayam+āviśya, simply joined; bibhartyavyaya is bibharti+avyayaḥ (-i+a-→-y a-).
#18
L: Since I am beyond the Perishable, and superior even to the Imperishable — therefore, in the world and in the Veda, I am celebrated [as] the Supreme Person.
I: Because I transcend the Perishable, and am higher even than the Imperishable, I am therefore celebrated, in the world and in the Veda, as the Supreme Person.
N: This is the chapter's title verse, Kṛṣṇa's own naming of himself as puruṣottamaḥ, 'the Supreme Person' (puruṣa uttama, 'highest of persons' — the very compound already used as a vocative address to Kṛṣṇa at 8.1, 10.15 and 11.3, now Kṛṣṇa's own declared identity, and the term that gives this chapter, Puruṣottama-yoga, its name): he stands beyond even the pairing of verses 16-17, atītaḥ kṣaram, 'transcending the Perishable' (the changing multiplicity of embodied beings), and uttamaḥ akṣarāt api, 'higher even than the Imperishable' (the unchanging individual self) — a third and highest term beyond both, prathitaḥ loke vede ca, 'renowned in the world and in the Veda'. Sandhi: yasmātkṣaram is yasmāt+kṣaram, simply joined (no change before k-); atīto'ham is atītaḥ+aham (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha); akṣarādapi is akṣarāt+api (-t+a-→-d a-, voicing before a vowel); cottamaḥ is ca+uttamaḥ (a+u→o); ato'smi is ataḥ+asmi (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha); puruṣottamaḥ is puruṣa+uttama (a+u→o).
#19
L: Who, thus undeluded, knows me [as] the Supreme Person — he, all-knowing, worships me with his whole being, O Bhārata.
I: Whoever, undeluded in this way, knows me as the Supreme Person, knows all there is to know, and worships me with his whole being, Bhārata.
N: This closes the puruṣottama teaching with its practical fruit: whoever mām evam asaṃmūḍhaḥ jānāti puruṣottamam, 'thus undeluded knows me as the Supreme Person' just declared in verse 18, becomes sa sarva-vit, 'a knower of all' (knowing the highest, he implicitly knows all that is derived from it, as at 7.2's yaj jñātvā neha bhūyo'nyaj jñātavyam avaśiṣyate), and bhajati mām sarva-bhāvena, 'worships me with his whole being' — undivided devotion again named as the fruit of the highest knowledge, as at 7.19's vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti sa mahātmā su-durlabhaḥ. Sandhi: māmevamasaṃmūḍho packs mām+evam (simply joined) and evam+asaṃmūḍhaḥ (simply joined), whose own -aḥ before j-→-o; puruṣottamam is puruṣa+uttamam (a+u→o); sarvavidbhajati is sarva-vit+bhajati (-t+bh-→-d bh-).
#20
L: Thus this most-secret teaching has been declared by me, O blameless one. Having understood this, one would become wise, and one who has accomplished his purpose, O Bhārata.
I: Thus have I declared this most secret teaching, blameless one. Understanding this, a person becomes wise, Bhārata, and has accomplished all that needs to be done.
N: This closes the chapter with a formal envoi typical of the Gītā's chapter-endings: iti guhyatamam śāstram, 'this most secret teaching' (guhyatama, superlative of guhya, 'secret', marking the puruṣottama doctrine of verses 16-19 as among the poem's innermost teachings, echoing 9.1's guhyāt guhyataram and anticipating 18.63's sarva-guhyatamam), has been uktam mayā, 'declared by me'; whoever etat buddhvā, 'having understood this', becomes buddhimān, 'wise, intelligent', and kṛta-kṛtyaḥ, 'one who has accomplished what was to be accomplished' (a set phrase for having fulfilled the whole purpose of life), closing the chapter on the promise already made, in different terms, at verse 19's fruit of undivided devotion. Sandhi: śāstramidamuktaṃ is śāstram+idam and idam+uktam, both simply joined (-m unaffected before the vowels i- and u-); mayānagha is mayā+anagha (ā+a→ā); etadbuddhvā is etat+buddhvā (-t+b-→-d b-); buddhimānsyāt is buddhimān+syāt, simply joined; kṛtakṛtyaśca is kṛtakṛtyaḥ+ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-).
